node.label: Glen Sean Coulthard
node.date_label: Subjects of Empire? (PhD) 2009 · Red Skin, White Masks 2014
node.description: A political theorist whose critique of recognition is read by historians of colonial Canada. His 2009 dissertation, the basis of Red Skin, White Masks (2014), set out 'to challenge the now commonplace assumption that the colonial relationship between Indigenous peoples and Canada can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon's critique of Hegel against the liberal recognition that Charles Taylor defended. Reworking Marx's primitive accumulation, he argued that 'the history and experience of dispossession, not proletarianization' had shaped relations with the Canadian state, and that Indigenous anti-colonialism is 'a struggle primarily inspired by and oriented around the question of land'. His alternative, self-recognition, means 'critically revaluating, reconstructing and redeploying Indigenous cultural forms'. He named Taiaiake Alfred, with James Tully, as a mentor.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Glen Sean Coulthard; Subjects of Empire? Indigenous Peoples and the 'Politics of Recognition' in Canada (PhD, University of Victoria, 2009); Red Skin, White Masks: Rejecting the Colonial Politics of Recognition (2014; foreword by Taiaiake Alfred).
node.scope_note: Read in part: the 2009 dissertation (abstract; introduction pp. 1–2, 11–20, 27–28; chapter openings pp. 74–75, 158–160). The 2014 book is unread at first hand; its p. 125 is known through Englert (2020). He builds on Canadian historians (Miller, Harris, Lutz) without criticising them in the pages read, and Wolfe is not cited there. In Canadian History PhDs: 27 citing theses; share 0 in 2000–09 and 3.6% in 2018–25 (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).

proposed_edges.relationship: Challenges 'the now commonplace assumption' that the colonial relationship between Indigenous peoples and Canada 'can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition'; liberal recognition 'can subtly reproduce non-mutual and unfree relations' (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, PhD dissertation (2009), abstract pp. iv–v and p. 28, where Taylor's 'The Politics of Recognition' (pp. 32–33) is quoted as the influential statement to be challenged; the 2014 book's subtitle, 'Rejecting the Colonial Politics of Recognition' (publisher). The book itself is unread at first hand. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Coulthard uses Fanon's critique of Hegel's master–slave dialectic against liberal recognition, while holding that Fanon's self-recognition 'fails to push us far enough' in settler states (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation pp. 27–28 (Fanon used against Hegel and liberal recognition) and p. 160: Fanon's notion of self-recognition 'remains an innovative and important contribution', but he was 'less willing to explore the role that these forms might play in providing substantive alternatives'. Influence with explicit qualification. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Reworks primitive accumulation, removing its 'excessively temporal framing' and developmental view: 'the history and experience of dispossession, not proletarianization' shaped relations between Indigenous peoples and the Canadian state (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation pp. 12–13 and 20; the 2014 book's 'place-based' reworking (publisher description). A critical reworking, not a rejection of Marx. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Defines colonial domination as power 'structured' to 'facilitate the dispossession of Indigenous peoples of their land and self-determining authority': 'Canada is no different than any other settler-colonial power' (2009); 'territorially acquisitive in perpetuity' (2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation p. 11; the 2014 book p. 125 as quoted by Englert (2020, read). Wolfe is not cited in the dissertation pages read; Englert's own critique of Wolfe is Englert's, not Coulthard's. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Self-recognition: 'critically revaluating, reconstructing and redeploying Indigenous cultural forms' to prefigure alternatives to colonial relations; Indigenous anti-colonialism 'oriented around the question of land' (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation abstract p. v and p. 20. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Coulthard cites Harris's 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess?' (2004) for the claim that after the fur trade Canada required 'first and foremost land, and only secondarily' Indigenous labour (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Dissertation p. 19 and n. 48. A supporting citation, not an acknowledged debt; held for stage 2. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

verification.note: UVic institutional repository PDF (issued 30 November 2009), read in part: abstract pp. iv–v; acknowledgements (Tully and Alfred as mentors); introduction pp. 1–2, 11–20, 27–28; chapter openings pp. 74–75 and 158–160. Passages used: 'to challenge the now commonplace assumption that the colonial relationship … can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition' (abstract); Taylor quoted as the influential statement (p. 28); 'Canada is no different than any other settler-colonial power' (p. 11); primitive accumulation's 'excessively temporal framing' (p. 13); 'dispossession, not proletarianization' (p. 20); Fanon 'fails to push us far enough' (p. 160). The 2014 book revises this text; quotations here are dated 2009. Wolfe is not cited in the pages read.

verification.note: Open access (CC BY-NC 3.0); pages 1, 3–4, 12–14, 17, 19–20 and 22–23 read. Resurgence 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions' and the turn from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy' toward 'a resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems' (p. 22); 'This colonial refusal should be met with Indigenous refusal' (p. 22), with n. 41 citing Coulthard on recognition and Audra Simpson on refusal; drafts reviewed outside standard academic peer review (n. 1). Passages reporting Elders' teachings and oral history are not used (OCAP limits).
